items.prompt: Per L1, what is a "termination meeting"?
choices: The short conversation where an already-final decision to end someone's employment is delivered — not a discussion or debate about whether it will happen
A meeting where the manager and the report jointly sit down and decide together whether to end the employment
The very first time any performance concerns are ever raised at all with the employee in question
A follow-up meeting held only after the employee has already physically left the company for good
items.explanation: L1 defines a termination meeting as the delivery of an already-final decision, not a discussion or negotiation about whether it happens.

items.prompt: Per L1, is the decision to terminate made during the termination meeting itself?
choices: No — the decision should already be final by the time this meeting happens, typically at the end of the PIP process
Yes — the entire point of holding the meeting is to make that final decision together, in the room
It depends entirely on how the employee happens to emotionally react during the meeting itself
L1 doesn't specify anywhere when exactly during the process the decision actually gets made
items.explanation: L1 is explicit that the decision should already be final before this meeting — it's where a decision is delivered, not made.

items.prompt: Per L1, is there a real trade-off between a termination being kind and being legally safe?
choices: No — most of what makes it feel humane (clarity, brevity, respect, no surprises) is also what makes it legally sound
Yes — a manager must always deliberately pick one priority or the other, never both at once
Yes, but only specifically in jurisdictions that don't recognize at-will employment
L1 deliberately doesn't take any position one way or the other on this particular question
items.explanation: L1's central claim is that this is a false trade-off — clarity and brevity serve both dignity and legal soundness at once.

choices: The specific, dated performance record, built during the PIP, that supports the decision if it is ever challenged
A verbal explanation given to the employee for the very first time during the termination meeting itself
A formal legal document that the employee signs agreeing in writing to their own termination
A general, unspecific statement noting only that performance simply wasn't good enough overall
items.explanation: L1 defines documented cause as the dated record built earlier, during the PIP — not something introduced fresh at the termination meeting.

items.prompt: Per L1, what does "dignity in the delivery" cover?
choices: The conversation itself and the practical details around it (timing, privacy, belongings, access), treated as owed to the person regardless of why the decision was made
Only whether the manager personally apologizes out loud to the person during the meeting itself
Whether or not the company decides to offer the departing employee any severance pay at all
Only the specific tone of voice the manager uses, not any of the surrounding practical logistics
items.explanation: L1 defines dignity in the delivery broadly — covering both the conversation and the surrounding practical details, not just tone.

items.prompt: Per L2, what does the "over-explain" instinct try to protect, and what actually goes wrong?
choices: It tries to protect the person's dignity, but can introduce undocumented justifications that contradict the record and create legal exposure
It tries to protect legal safety specifically, but ends up feeling unexpectedly cold and sudden to the person
It carries no real risk at all — L2 actually recommends over-explaining to the person whenever possible
It tries mainly to protect the manager's own personal reputation among the rest of the team
items.explanation: L2's table pairs over-explaining with the dignity instinct, and its risk with introducing off-the-cuff justifications that don't match the documented record.

items.prompt: Per L2, what does the "under-explain" instinct try to protect, and what actually goes wrong?
choices: It tries to protect legal safety, but can feel cold and sudden even after a properly run PIP
It tries to protect the person's dignity, but ends up creating legal exposure
It has no real downside at all, according to L2's own framework for how this should go
It only actually applies in jurisdictions that specifically lack at-will employment protections
items.explanation: L2's table pairs under-explaining with the legal-safety instinct, noting the risk of feeling cold and sudden despite a fair underlying process.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, why does the decision get stated first, in the first minute, with no preamble?
choices: Delaying it stretches out the moment the person realizes what's happening, which is worse for dignity, not better
It's treated as a formal legal requirement that applies the same way in every single jurisdiction
It gives the manager more personal time to think carefully about what to say next in the room
It allows the person being let go more time to prepare a considered rebuttal to the decision
items.explanation: L2 explains that a preamble stretches out the moment of realization rather than sparing the person anything — stating it first is what respects them.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does the reason given in the meeting stay to one sentence, tied to the PIP, instead of a fuller account of every issue?
choices: Every reason given becomes part of the record, and introducing a new reason not part of the documented PIP process creates a mismatch that is exactly the legal exposure being avoided
Stating the reason in exactly one sentence is itself treated as a formal legal requirement
The manager simply doesn't actually know any more detailed reasons behind the decision
Giving several more detailed reasons would make the meeting feel more comforting to the person
items.explanation: L2 explains that anything said in this room becomes part of the record — a new, undocumented reason is the over-explaining failure mode in practice.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's wrong with treating the meeting as a debate to be won if the person disagrees?
choices: It reopens exactly the discussion the PIP process was designed to have already concluded
It's not actually treated as a failure mode at all — L2 recommends debating firmly if challenged
It's only considered a problem if nobody from HR happens to be present in the room at the time
It only really matters in jurisdictions that have unusually strong employee protection laws
items.explanation: L2 states directly that turning the meeting into a debate reopens the discussion the PIP process already concluded, undermining the whole point of the prior process.

items.prompt: Per L3, what three practical things does the manager need ready before the meeting, beyond the opening line?
choices: Confirmation of the last working day, pay/benefits details (or when they'll follow), and equipment/access logistics
A written legal defense of the decision, a signed witness statement, and a severance calculator spreadsheet
A completed performance review, a written reference letter, and a prepared exit interview script
Nothing at all beyond the opening line — L3 says the rest of the meeting can simply be improvised
items.explanation: L3's table lists last working day, pay and benefits, and access/equipment as the specific practical items to prepare in advance.

items.prompt: In L3's scripted opening, how quickly does the manager state the actual decision?
choices: Almost immediately — within the first minute, with no softening preamble
Only after roughly a 10-minute discussion recapping the person's recent performance history
Only after the person being let go directly asks what the meeting is actually about
At the very end of the meeting, only after every practical logistic has already been covered
items.explanation: L3's script has the manager stating the decision within the first minute, consistent with L2's "no preamble" principle.

items.prompt: In L3, what does the manager cite as the basis for the decision?
choices: The specific written PIP expectations from the previous unit, and that they weren't met by the June 30 checkpoint
A long, itemized list covering every individual performance frustration from the past two full quarters
The report's general personality and overall attitude, described broadly rather than specifically
Nothing specific at all — the manager deliberately avoids giving any concrete reason whatsoever
items.explanation: L3's script ties the reason directly and specifically to the PIP's written expectations and the June 30 checkpoint — one sentence, tied to the documented record.

items.prompt: When the report pushes back in L3 ("you never really gave me a real chance"), how does the manager respond?
choices: Acknowledges the feeling, restates the documented basis once, briefly, and declines to relitigate it further
Offers a longer, much more detailed defense covering every individual step of the entire PIP process
Apologizes on the spot and immediately reverses the termination decision in the room
Ends the meeting immediately and walks out without responding to the pushback at all
items.explanation: L3's script has the manager acknowledge the feeling, restate the reason once, and explicitly decline to relitigate — matching L2's guidance.

items.prompt: What does the flat line at zero in L3's chart of "new justifications introduced" actually represent?
choices: That the number of new reasons given stays at zero throughout the conversation, including under pushback — the concrete version of "don't relitigate"
That the manager gave zero explanation of any kind to the person, at any point in the meeting
That the entire termination meeting lasted exactly zero minutes from start to finish
That the report accepted the decision completely immediately, with absolutely zero pushback
items.explanation: L3 explains the chart's flat line is the checkable version of the principle that no new justifications get introduced, even when challenged.

items.prompt: Per L3's "extend it" question, what changes when the news is a layoff affecting several people rather than one performance-based termination?
choices: The reason shifts from individual documented cause to a business-driven decision, and practical details expand to include severance terms and coordinated timing across multiple conversations
Nothing changes at all in this situation — the exact same script applies word for word either way
The core structure (decision first, one reason, don't relitigate) stops applying entirely in this case
Only the practical logistics change in this case; the reason given still stays about individual performance
items.explanation: L3 explains the core structure holds, but the reason becomes business-driven rather than individual cause, and the scope of preparation expands significantly.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure modes, what role does a second person (typically HR) in the room play?
choices: Acts as a witness and handles questions the manager isn't the right person to answer, helping avoid over-explaining under pressure
Delivers the entire termination meeting personally so the manager doesn't have to speak at all
Has no real function in the room beyond simply making it feel more crowded during the conversation
Is only ever required in meetings involving termination for cause, never in layoff situations
items.explanation: L3 explains the second person's value as both a witness and a resource for questions outside the manager's role, which helps prevent improvised over-explaining.
